systems.name: Iterated maps
systems.summary: A few moves, each one shrinking, turning and shifting the plane, applied to one point again and again in random order. The points pile up on one fixed shape, such as a fern

blocks.label: One move
blocks.tex: f_k(x,y) = \bigl(a_k x + b_k y + e_k,\; c_k x + d_k y + f_k\bigr)
blocks.note: Move number k takes the point (x, y) to a new point. The letter f on the left is the move's name. The numbers a, b, c, d shrink, stretch and turn, and the numbers e, f shift. For example a = d = 0.5 with the rest 0 halves the distance of every point from the centre

blocks.label: Picking the moves at random
blocks.note: z with a small n below it is the point after n steps. At each step one move is picked at random, move k with probability p (its chance, from 0 to 1), and applied to the point. This random walk is called the chaos game

blocks.label: The shape the points settle on
blocks.note: A is the shape. Applying every move to the whole shape and putting the pieces together gives the same shape again, which is why a fern is made of smaller ferns. A shape that the points are drawn to like this is called an attractor

blocks.label: Why the points settle on one shape
blocks.note: M is the table of the four numbers a, b, c, d of move k, and s is the most that the move can stretch a length. The square root is the standard way to compute s from the four numbers. When s is below 1 for every move, every move shrinks distances, so the points end on the same shape from any starting point

dimension.label: Dimension, measured by counting boxes
dimension.note: The shape is covered by a grid of squares of side epsilon, and N is the number of squares that hold part of it. When the squares get smaller, N grows: for a line, halving the side doubles N, and d = 1; for a filled area, it multiplies N by four, and d = 2. The fern measures about 1.78

systems.name: Rewriting systems
systems.summary: A short word of letters rewritten by a few rules, all letters at once, several times over. The final word is then read as orders for a drawing pen, and it draws a plant, a curve or a snowflake

blocks.label: One rewriting pass
blocks.note: Omega is one letter and omega prime, written with a small stroke, is what replaces it. w with a small n below it is the word after n passes, and P is one pass: every letter is replaced at the same time. So the number of F letters is multiplied by the same number at every pass, by 4 for the Koch curve

blocks.label: The rules of the branching plant
blocks.note: Every X becomes F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X and every F becomes FF. F draws one step, plus and minus turn by the angle. An opening bracket saves the place of the pen and the closing one brings it back, which makes a side branch

blocks.label: How the pen moves
blocks.note: p with a small n below it is the place of the pen after n orders, and theta is its direction. Each F moves the pen one step of length l in that direction. Each plus or minus changes the direction by the angle alpha, the same angle for the whole word. A drawing pen moved like this is called a turtle

dimension.label: Dimension, read from the rule
dimension.note: When a shape is made of N exact copies of itself, each s times its size, its dimension is d = log N / log(1/s). The Koch curve is 4 copies at a third of the size, so d = log 4 / log 3, about 1.262: 3 raised to the power 1.262 gives 4

systems.name: Dielectric breakdown
systems.summary: How does a spark choose its path through glass or wood? Such a material does not conduct electricity, and is called a dielectric. When a strong enough voltage burns a path through it, this is called dielectric breakdown. The model splits the material into square cells. The spark starts from one cell and burns one more cell at a time. A cell next to the tips of the burn, where the electric field is strongest, is the most likely to burn next. The result is a branching mark like the one a real spark leaves

blocks.label: The voltage around the burn
blocks.note: φ (phi) is the voltage at a cell. The burn conducts electricity, so its voltage is 0 all along it. The outer edge of the block, or the far plate, is held at voltage 1. The equation ∇²φ = 0 says that the voltage at every other cell equals the average of the voltages around it

blocks.label: Which cell burns next
blocks.note: p_i is the chance that cell i burns next. Only cells touching the burn can be chosen, and the sum below the line runs over all of them, so the chances add up to 1. |∇φ_i| is the electric field at cell i: how sharply the voltage changes there. It is raised to the power η (eta). With η = 1, a cell with twice the field is twice as likely to burn next. With η = 2 it is four times as likely. With η = 0 every cell is equally likely

blocks.label: How the program finds the voltage
blocks.note: φ with (m) above it is the voltage after m rounds; r and c are the row and column of a cell. In each round every cell takes the average of its four neighbours: above, below, left and right. At the start the rounds are repeated until the numbers stop changing. After each new burned cell, a few more rounds bring the voltage up to date

dimension.label: The dimension depends on the power η
dimension.note: Dimension says how fully the burn fills the flat block: 1 for a line, 2 for a filled area. With η = 0.6 the burn measures 1.58, with η = 2 it measures 1.27. A dense bush fills more of the block than a thin bolt, so it measures higher

systems.name: Wandering particles
systems.summary: What shape grows when particles wander at random and stick where they land? One particle is fixed at the centre of a square grid. Other particles are released one at a time. Each one moves by random steps until it lands next to a particle already in place, and then it stays there. The clump of stuck particles is called the cluster. It grows thin branching arms. The process is called diffusion-limited aggregation. Random wandering of particles is called diffusion, and the particles gather, or aggregate, only as fast as their wandering brings them

blocks.label: One random step
blocks.note: (y, x) is the cell where the particle stands: row y, column x. Pr means the chance. The particle moves one cell up, down, left or right, each with chance 1/4. It prefers no direction and does not remember its earlier steps

blocks.label: When a particle stops
blocks.tex: \text{stop at the first site with a neighbour already in the cluster}
blocks.note: A particle stops at the first cell next to the cluster. A wandering particle almost always meets the tips of the arms first, so the gaps between the arms stay nearly empty

blocks.label: How the count of particles grows with distance
blocks.tex: N(r) = k\,r^{d} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \log N = d \log r + \log k
blocks.note: N(r) is the number of particles within r cells of the centre, k is a fixed number, and d is the dimension. For a filled disc d = 2: twice the radius holds four times the particles. For a line d = 1. A logarithm counts powers: in base 10, log 100 = 2 and log 1000 = 3. Drawn with log N up and log r across, the counts lie on a straight line, and its slope is d

dimension.label: Dimension of the cluster
dimension.note: Measured on this page: about 1.67. For very large clusters the value approaches 1.71. A small cluster gives a value lower than a large one

systems.name: Julia sets
systems.summary: Which starting points stay near the centre forever when one step is repeated without end? Each point of the plane is written as a number with two parts: how far across and how far up. Such a number is called a complex number. Its two parts are joined by the letter i, a number whose square is minus one. The step squares the point's number and adds a fixed number c. The result is the next point, and the step is repeated on it. Some starting points stay near the centre. Others move further away with every step and never come back: they escape. The points that never escape form a filled shape, and its edge is called the Julia set of c. The page starts at c = -0.5 + 0.5i. The two c sliders change c, and the big picture shows the shape for that c. The thing to watch: for some c the shape is one piece, for others it falls apart into dust

blocks.label: The step that is repeated
blocks.note: z is the current point, written as a complex number, and n counts the steps. Squaring z doubles its angle around the centre and squares its distance from the centre. Adding c then shifts it by a fixed amount. Example with c = 0: the point 0.5 goes to 0.25, then to 0.0625

blocks.label: The shape of the points that stay
blocks.note: K_c is the set of starting points z_0 for which the distance |z_n| from the centre never grows without limit. The Julia set is the edge of this shape

blocks.label: When a point counts as escaped
blocks.note: Once a point is more than 2 away from the centre, every later step takes it further, and it never comes back. So one step past 2 is enough to stop and mark the point as escaped. This is what lets a computer draw the picture in a limited number of steps

blocks.label: Without the added number, the edge is a plain circle
blocks.note: With c = 0 the step only squares. A point closer than 1 to the centre shrinks towards 0. A point further than 1 grows without limit. The edge between them is the circle of radius 1, a smooth curve. The added number c is what makes the edge rough

dimension.label: How rough the edge is: its dimension
dimension.note: Dimension measures roughness here. A smooth curve has dimension 1, a filled area has dimension 2. It is found by covering the edge with small squares and counting how fast their number grows as the squares shrink. In the formula, dim_B is this box-counting dimension and ∂K_c is the edge of K_c. For a Julia set the result lies between 1 and 2. It depends on c and reaches 2 for some values of c

systems.name: The Mandelbrot set
systems.summary: Start from 0, square, add a fixed number c, and repeat: for which c does the result stay near 0 forever? Each point of the plane is written as a complex number: a number with two parts, how far across and how far up, joined by the letter i, a number whose square is minus one. Each point of this picture is one value of c. For each c the computer starts from 0 and repeats the step. If the result stays within 2 of the centre for every step tried, c belongs to the Mandelbrot set and is drawn in the solid tone. If it escapes past 2, c is shaded by how many steps that took. The same values of c decide another picture, the Julia set of c: it holds together in one piece exactly when c is in the Mandelbrot set. The view starts centred on -0.6 with half the width of the view at 1.6. A click centres the picture and the zoom slider magnifies it. The thing to watch: at every zoom the edge shows new detail

blocks.label: Which c belong to the set
blocks.note: M is the set of numbers c for which the repeated step, started from z_0 = 0, never takes the point infinitely far away. The bars |z_n| mean the distance of z_n from the centre. One picture answers the question for every c at once

blocks.label: The link with Julia sets
blocks.note: For a fixed c, K_c is the shape formed by the starting points that never escape, and its edge is the Julia set. K_c is one connected piece exactly when c is in the Mandelbrot set. For c outside, it breaks into separate specks, like dust

blocks.label: How the outside is shaded
blocks.note: nu(c), written with the Greek letter nu, counts the steps until the point first gets further than R from the centre. R is the escape distance, 2 on this page. The bands of shade in the picture are bands of equal count

dimension.label: The roughness of the edge, proved rather than measured
dimension.note: Dimension measures roughness: a smooth curve has dimension 1, a filled area has 2. dim_H is one exact way of measuring it, and ∂M is the edge of the Mandelbrot set. It has been proved that this edge has dimension 2, the most a curve in the plane can have. No picture with a limited number of pixels can show this limit

systems.name: The three-dimensional set
systems.summary: Is there a solid in space built the way the Mandelbrot set is built? The flat Mandelbrot set comes from one step: square a point of the plane, add a fixed point c, repeat from 0, and keep the c for which the point never runs off. Squaring a point of the plane squares its distance from the centre and doubles its angle. A point in space has a distance r from the centre and two angles. This solid replaces squaring with a power n: the distance is raised to the power n and both angles are multiplied by n. Then c is added, and the step is repeated. The points that never run off form the solid on the screen, drawn at power 8. The camera circles it. The thing to watch: the number of folds around the vertical axis is one fewer than the power

blocks.label: Raising a point of space to a power
blocks.tex: \mathbf{v}^{n} = r^{n}\bigl(\sin n\theta \cos n\varphi,\; \sin n\theta \sin n\varphi,\; \cos n\theta \bigr)
blocks.note: v is a point of space. r is its distance from the centre. Theta is its angle down from the vertical axis, phi its angle around that axis. Raising v to the power n raises r to the power n and multiplies both angles by n. In the plane, squaring does the same with the power 2

blocks.label: The step that is repeated
blocks.note: k counts the steps. Each step raises the point to the power n and adds a fixed point c. The points c for which the repeated step never runs off to infinity form the solid. At n = 8 the solid has seven identical folds around its axis, one fewer than the power

blocks.label: How the computer finds the surface
blocks.note: The picture is drawn by sending a ray from the eye through each pixel. DE, the distance estimate, says how far the ray still is from the surface. It is worked out from the point v and from v', which says how fast v changes when the starting point moves a little. The ray can move forward by DE without passing through the surface, so it reaches the surface in a few long steps

dimension.label: How rough the surface is
dimension.note: Dimension measures roughness. A smooth surface has dimension 2, a filled solid has 3. In the formula, dim_B is the dimension found by counting small boxes, and ∂ is the surface of the solid. The surface of this solid lies between the two. It is a rough surface, not a curve

systems.name: Does a river remember its past years? The Hurst exponent
systems.summary: A line built from random steps that remember the steps before them. One number, H, says how strong the memory is, and Hurst measured it on the Nile. The same number gives the roughness of the line.

blocks.label: Steps that remember
blocks.note: Rho of k is the correlation between two steps k places apart: a number from -1 to 1 that says how much one tends to follow the other. The formula is for fractional Gaussian noise, the steps of a walk with memory. H = 0.5 gives zero, a coin toss with no memory. Above 0.5 a run tends to continue; below it a run tends to reverse.

blocks.label: Hurst's rescaled range
blocks.note: In a block of m steps, R is how far the running sum ranges, from its highest to its lowest point, and S is how much the single steps vary. Their ratio grows like m to the power H. Hurst found 0.72 across the Nile and seventy-four other records, where a coin gives 0.5.

blocks.label: The spread of the future
blocks.note: Sigma of T is how far the walk may be T steps ahead, and sigma alone is the typical size of one step. For a coin toss the spread grows like the square root of T. A series with memory spreads faster, so a long time ahead is riskier than the square-root rule says.

blocks.label: Roughness of the line
blocks.note: D is the box-counting dimension of the walk drawn as a line: the line is covered with small squares, and the count of squares it touches is followed as the squares shrink. D is 1 for a smooth line and close to 2 for a line so rough that it almost fills an area. A walk whose runs go on draws a smoother line; a walk whose runs reverse draws a rougher one. A coastline is measured the same way.

dimension.label: What it cannot do
dimension.note: The formula says that knowing the present value barely changes the expected next one. H describes how risk grows with the time ahead and whether runs continue, not what the next value will be. H is also hard to read from a short series: this was Lo's objection in 1991.

systems.name: How much to trust a new customer's own record
systems.summary: An insurer's price for a new customer mixes the customer's short record with the group's long one. The share given to the record is called the credibility. When claims arrive at random and the rates across customers follow a gamma curve, this mix is exactly what Bayes' rule for updating a belief gives.

blocks.label: The mix
blocks.note: Lambda hat is the estimated claim rate. X bar is the customer's own average number of claims a year over n years, and mu is the group's average rate. Z is the weight on the customer's record: it rises from zero towards one as the years come. Whitney 1918, Bailey 1950, Buhlmann 1967.

blocks.label: What k means
blocks.note: k is the noise in one customer's results divided by the spread between customers; Var means variance, a measure of spread. When customers differ a lot from each other, k is small and a record earns its own rate quickly. When one customer's results are noisy, k is large and the record earns it slowly. Z is one half when n = k.

blocks.label: The exact calculation behind it
blocks.tex: \lambda \sim \Gamma(a, b),\quad X \mid \lambda \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda) \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda \mid x \sim \Gamma(a + x,\, b + n)
blocks.note: Before any record, the customer's rate lambda is believed to follow a gamma curve with parameters a and b. Claims follow a Poisson model with that rate. After x claims in n years the belief is again a gamma curve, with parameters a + x and b + n. Its centre, (a + x) / (b + n), is the same mix with k = b and mu = a / b. The page draws this belief as a curve that narrows year by year.

dimension.label: The same mix in other actuarial work
dimension.note: Money set aside for claims not yet paid is mixed the same way, from the year's own pattern (the chain ladder) and an expectation fixed in advance, with the share already reported as Z. Forecasts of how long people live widen their ranges in the same way when the model's numbers are uncertain.

systems.name: When one claim outweighs a thousand
systems.summary: Insurance claims whose sizes follow a Pareto tail: most are small, a few are enormous, and the large ones thin out the same way at every size. The tail index alpha plays the part that a dimension plays for a coastline. Below alpha of two the average never settles.

blocks.label: The tail
blocks.note: P(X > x) is the probability that a claim X is larger than x; x0 is the smallest possible claim and alpha the tail index. On log-log axes this is a straight line with slope minus alpha, where a thin tail bends down. Pareto found the same law for incomes in 1896.

blocks.label: The same at every scale
blocks.note: Given that a claim is above a threshold u, the chance that it is above x follows the same law with the same alpha. So the largest tenth of the claims, rescaled, is spread like all of them. This is self-similarity, the same shape at every scale, as for a coastline.

blocks.label: The average that never settles
blocks.note: E[X] is the average claim, finite only when alpha is above 1. Var[X] is the variance, how far claims stray from the average; it is infinite when alpha is 2 or less. Then one claim can outweigh all the earlier ones, Mandelbrot's Noah effect, and the running average keeps jumping however many claims arrive.

dimension.label: The tail index as a dimension
dimension.note: Alpha is read from the slope of the chart of P(X > x) against x on log-log axes, as a dimension is read from the slope of a box count. Both are exponents of a power law: they say how a count changes with scale.

definitions.name: Dimension by counting boxes
definitions.note: A grid of square boxes, each with side ε (epsilon), is laid over the shape. N(ε) is the number of boxes the shape touches. As the boxes shrink, N grows, and the dimension d says how fast. In words: d is the logarithm of the count divided by the logarithm of 1/ε, as ε goes to zero. A logarithm finds a power, so this asks: to what power must the shrink factor be raised to give the growth of the count? With a number: if halving the boxes multiplies the count by 2.83, then d = 1.5, because 2 to the power 1.5 is 2.83. A line gives d = 1 and a filled square d = 2.

definitions.name: Dimension of a shape made of copies of itself
definitions.note: Some shapes are made of exactly N copies of themselves, each shrunk by the factor s. Then N times s to the power d equals 1, which gives d = log N / log(1/s), where log is the logarithm. With numbers: the Koch curve is N = 4 copies, each s = 1/3 of its size. So 3 to the power d must equal 4, and d = log 4 / log 3, about 1.262.

definitions.name: Hausdorff dimension
definitions.note: The strictest definition of dimension. The shape S is covered by small pieces U_i, each with a diameter, its widest span, of at most δ (delta). Each diameter is raised to a power p, and the results are added. As δ goes to zero, this sum, written H^p(S), grows without limit when p is too small and falls to zero when p is too large. The dimension d is the power where it switches, the smallest p that gives zero. Box counting gives an estimate of this number.

definitions.name: Dimension from walking dividers
definitions.note: Dividers, two legs set a fixed distance ε apart, are walked along a curve, and the steps are added up to a length L(ε). On a smooth curve L hardly changes as ε shrinks. On a rough curve L grows in proportion to ε to the power 1 - d, where d is the dimension. With a number: for the coast of Britain d = 1.232, so halving the opening makes the measured length about 1.17 times as long, since 2 to the power 0.232 is 1.17.
